title: Thinking Out Loud and Structuring Your Code
summary: Narrating your approach and structuring code into small, named pieces so the interviewer can follow, and credit, your thinking, not just your final answer.

slides.markdown:
An interviewer can't grade a solution that only exists inside your head. **Everything they credit - the approach, the trade-offs you weighed, the bug you caught - has to be said out loud or written down**, or as far as they're concerned it didn't happen.

This is why two candidates who arrive at the same working code can get very different scores: one narrated a clear line of reasoning the whole way, the other went quiet for six minutes and produced the answer as if by magic. The silent one gets credit for the output. The narrating one gets credit for the thinking, which is what the interview is actually measuring.

This topic is about what to say, when to say it, and how to structure code so the narration and the code reinforce each other instead of competing.

slides.subTitle: Approach, then complexity, then code
slides.markdown:
A simple loop covers most of an interview: **state your approach in one or two sentences, state its complexity, then start writing code.** Repeat the loop whenever you change direction.

"I'll use a hash set to track numbers I've seen, so I can check for a complement in O(1) - that gets the whole pass to O(n) time, O(n) space." That single sentence tells the interviewer what you're building and why, before they've watched a single character of code.

The loop matters more once you're partway through: if you realize your first approach doesn't handle duplicates, say so - "actually, this breaks with duplicate keys, let me adjust" - rather than silently rewriting and hoping they notice the fix instead of the initial gap.

The single most common way narration fails: going quiet for several minutes while you work out the entire solution in your head, then dictating a finished answer as if it arrived instantly.

From the interviewer's side this looks identical whether you're deeply stuck or one insight away - they have no way to distinguish "thinking productively" from "stalled," and both read as risk. It also throws away partial credit: if you're silently 80% of the way to a working approach when time runs out, a silent candidate gets scored on the 0% they said, not the 80% they privately reached.

The fix isn't narrating every micro-thought - it's narrating **state**, every 20-30 seconds: "I'm trying to see if sorting first helps... it does, because then the two pointers can move toward each other." A short, real-time trace beats a long silence followed by a monologue.

slides.subTitle: i, j, tmp, flag vs. real names
slides.markdown:
Under time pressure it's tempting to write `i`, `j`, `tmp`, and `flag` everywhere. Resist it for anything that isn't a pure loop index - a variable name is free narration that survives even if you stop talking.

Compare `left`, `right`, `windowSum`, and `seen` against `i`, `j`, `s`, and `m`. The first set tells the interviewer what the algorithm is doing without another word of explanation; the second forces them to reconstruct your intent from context, exactly when they're also trying to track whether your logic is correct.

`i` and `j` are fine for a genuine array index in a simple loop - that's idiomatic, not lazy. The rule is really about anything that holds a *concept*: a running total, a seen-set, a boolean that means something specific. Name the concept, not the type.

Decomposing your solution into a few small named functions - `isValid(window)`, `mergeIntervals(list)` - keeps partial progress visible and gradable, even if you run out of time before wiring everything together.

A single 40-line function that's two-thirds done looks like an unfinished mess. The same logic split into three 12-line helper functions, two of which are complete and correct, looks like real, partial, creditable progress - because the interviewer can read each piece independently and see exactly which part works.

This also makes your own narration easier: "I'll write `hasCycle` first, assuming a valid graph, then handle the invalid case separately" is a plan you can say in one sentence and a shape the interviewer can follow slide by slide as you fill it in.

slides.subTitle: When detail drowns the signal
slides.markdown:
The opposite failure of going silent: narrating every micro-step so thoroughly that the interviewer can no longer tell which sentence carries the actual decision.

"So now I'm going to declare a variable, and I'll call it count, and I'll set it to zero, and now I'm going to open a for loop that goes from zero up to the length of the array..." - none of this is wrong, but none of it is a decision either. It's transcription, not narration, and it buries the one sentence that mattered ("I chose a hash map here instead of sorting because I need this in one pass") under ten that didn't.

Narrate **decisions and their reasons** - why this data structure, why this order of operations, why this edge case needs a branch. Let mechanical code, like a loop or an increment, speak for itself.

slides.sectionTitle: Brute force first, or silently jump to optimal?
slides.subTitle: Naming the baseline earns you the credit for improving on it
slides.markdown:
Two ways to open a solution to the same problem:

- **Mention the brute force first, briefly, then improve on it out loud.** "The obvious approach is checking every pair, O(n squared). I can do better with a hash set - one pass, O(n)." This takes ten seconds and gives the interviewer a baseline to measure your optimization against.
- **Jump straight to the optimal approach with no baseline stated.** The final complexity might be identical, but the interviewer has no visibility into whether you actually *saw* the naive approach and improved on it, or arrived at the optimal one by pattern-matching without understanding the trade-off you made.

Naming the brute force isn't slower in practice - it's one sentence - and it's the difference between "knows there's a better way and can say why" and "produced the right answer, mechanism unclear."

The senior move is naming a limitation of your own solution **before** the interviewer has to point it out: "this is O(n squared) as written; I can get it to O(n log n) with a sort first, if that's worth the extra code."

This does two things a purely correct, silent solution doesn't: it shows you can evaluate your own work critically, which is a large part of what distinguishes a strong mid-level engineer from a senior one, and it hands the interviewer a natural branch point - they can say "sure, show me," or "that's fine, let's move on," instead of having to spend their own time diagnosing the gap.

Waiting to be asked "can this be faster?" and only then explaining the optimization is strictly worse than volunteering it - even though the code produced is identical either way.

slides.subTitle: Same code, with and without narration
slides.markdown:
```
# Without narration - the interviewer sees only this, four minutes later:
def two_sum(nums, target):
    seen = {}
    for i, x in enumerate(nums):
        if target - x in seen:
            return [seen[target - x], i]
        seen[x] = i

# With narration, said aloud while typing the same code:
# "Brute force is checking every pair, O(n squared). I can do better -
#  a hash map from value to index lets me check for the complement in
#  O(1), so one pass gets this to O(n) time, O(n) space."
# ... writes the loop ...
# "seen holds every number I've placed so far, keyed by value, so this
#  check is asking: have I already seen the number that completes target?"
```

The code is identical. The score isn't - the second version demonstrates the reasoning the first one only implies.

slides.sectionTitle: Pacing the narration under real time pressure
slides.subTitle: The senior-level nuance
slides.markdown:
Early on, narrate generously - every approach, every trade-off, every named variable's intent - because the interviewer is still forming a model of how you think. As the clock runs down and you're implementing a plan you've already sold, narration can compress: shorter status pings ("handling the base case now... done, recursing") replace full sentences, because the interviewer already has the mental model and doesn't need it rebuilt every ten seconds.

The skill that separates a senior candidate here is recognizing **which** silence is safe. Silence while typing out an agreed, well-understood plan reads fine. Silence while you're privately reconsidering the whole approach reads as risk - that's exactly the moment to say "actually, hold on, let me reconsider this" rather than let the pause speak for itself.

Thinking out loud is the delivery mechanism for two skills covered elsewhere in this group: naming your own complexity trade-offs as you build (see `complexity-tradeoff-communication`), and recognizing which technique a problem calls for before you start narrating it (see `pattern-recognition-framework`). Both depend on you actually saying the reasoning, not just having it.

It also sets up what happens when the narration reveals you're stuck - covered in `handling-being-stuck` - where the same habit of stating what you've ruled out, rather than going silent, is what turns a stall into a recoverable moment instead of a collapse.
